The chord in question contains these intervals, making it an augmented triad.

Proper spacing requires that adjacent upper voices be no more than an octave apart, while the bass can be any distance from the tenor. When the distance between soprano and alto, or alto and tenor, exceeds an octave, this creates incorrect spacing that produces a hollow or unbalanced sound. Segment B contains voices in the upper parts that are spaced more than an octave apart, violating this fundamental principle of voice leading. This is a fundamental error in common practice harmony because the dissonant seventh creates tension that demands resolution. The seventh must resolve down by step, typically to the third of the following chord, to satisfy the harmonic expectations established in tonal music. The correct answer is an unresolved seventh because segment C contains a seventh that fails to resolve downward by step as required by standard voice leading principles.

Topic:2.6: Interval Inversion and Compound Intervals
q.ex: When inverting an interval, the original interval and its inversion always sum to nine. To find the quality of the inverted interval, major intervals invert to minor intervals and vice versa, diminished intervals invert to augmented intervals and vice versa, and perfect intervals remain perfect. Since the correct answer is a major third, the original interval must have been a minor sixth, as a sixth inverts to a third (6 + 3 = 9) and minor inverts to major. The correct choice is a major third because it represents the proper inversion where the interval size changes from sixth to third and the quality changes from minor to major.

q.ex: Largo indicates the slowest tempo among these options. In standard musical tempo markings from slowest to fastest, Largo (meaning "broad" in Italian) is one of the slowest tempos, typically ranging from 40-60 beats per minute. Adagio is slow but slightly faster than Largo, Andantino is moderately slow (a walking pace), and Allegro is fast and lively. Therefore, Largo is correct because it represents the broadest, most expansive tempo marking of the four choices.

Simple meters have beats that divide into two equal parts, while compound meters divide into three. The terms duple, triple, and quadruple refer to two, three, or four beats per measure respectively. Simple triple meter contains three beats per measure with each beat dividing into two parts, typically notated as 3/4 or 3/8 time signatures. q.ex: A half cadence is a cadence that ends on the dominant (V) chord, creating a sense of pause or incompleteness that requires continuation. This type of cadence functions as a musical question mark, leaving the phrase harmonically open rather than resolved. In contrast, an authentic cadence moves from V to I (providing full closure), a plagal cadence moves from IV to I (the "Amen" cadence), and a deceptive cadence moves from V to a chord other than I, typically vi. The excerpt ends with a half cadence because it concludes on the dominant chord, creating harmonic tension that anticipates further musical material.

In music theory, closely related keys are those that differ from the tonic by no more than one sharp or flat in their key signatures. A minor triad consists of a root, a minor third above the root (three half steps), and a perfect fifth above the root (seven half steps). q.ex: In music, text setting refers to how syllables of text align with musical notes. Syllabic text setting means each syllable of text is matched with a single note, creating a one-to-one correspondence. This contrasts with melismatic setting, where a single syllable is sung across multiple notes. When a vocal melody is primarily syllabic, the text moves efficiently with the music, with most syllables receiving their own individual pitch. The correct answer is that the text setting is primarily syllabic because the vocal melody assigns one note per syllable for most of the passage.
